result:
There was a man in our building who practiced applause.

Every evening at six, just as the pipes began knocking with everyone’s dinner water, he would clap for twenty minutes. Sometimes slowly, with the solemnity of a visiting dignitary. Sometimes in quick, delighted bursts. Sometimes there was a pause followed by a tremendous renewal, as though someone had returned to the stage.

He lived directly below me.

For three weeks I hated him without knowing his face.

I was studying for an examination I had already failed twice. My desk stood over the place where, I imagined, he kept his chair. At six I would be reading the same paragraph about municipal drainage, and beneath me a roomful of invisible people would apparently learn that the war was over.

I tried earplugs. I moved to the kitchen. Finally, I went downstairs.

He opened the door wearing a cardigan with one sleeve neatly pinned at the elbow.

This complicated my complaint.

Behind him, on a table, was a wooden contraption: a hinged arm, a pedal, and what looked like a padded leather paddle.

“Yes?” he said.

“I’m upstairs.”

“Ah.”

“The noise.”

He glanced back at the apparatus.

“I can do it earlier.”

“What is it?”

“A hand.”

I looked again.

“My daughter made it,” he said. “She works in theatrical properties. Mostly swords. You’d be surprised how many swords they get through.”

He showed me how it worked. His foot pressed the pedal, raising the padded piece. His remaining hand met it.

Clap.

The sound was ordinary. That seemed, somehow, the strangest part.

“Is it for exercise?” I asked.

“No. I go to things.”

He pointed toward a noticeboard crowded with tickets.

School concerts. Amateur plays. A lecture about bats. A poetry reading at the library.

“My wife used to handle this side of things,” he said, nodding toward his missing arm.

I must have looked confused, because he demonstrated: one hand held out toward an absent person.

“She’d lend me hers. We got quite good.”

I said I was sorry, and he said thank you, and neither of us specified for what.

“I’ve been practicing for our grandson’s recital. First time I’ll take the thing out.” He bent to adjust a strap. “It has to sit on my knee without sliding. And I don’t want to get carried away and stamp on the pedal. Makes an awful bang on a wooden floor.”

We settled on five-thirty.

For the next month, his applause became part of my timetable. I ate something before it began. When it stopped, I made coffee and opened the drainage manual.

I passed the examination in November.

Coming home, I found him in the lobby, attempting to carry a bag of oranges and retrieve his keys.

“How did it go?” he asked.

I hadn’t realized he knew the date.

“I passed.”

He put the oranges down.

There was a brief, awkward interval in which his hand moved, then stopped.

“Hang on,” he said. “Come upstairs.”

“You don’t have to.”

“I know where I keep the biscuits, too.”

So I followed him.

He gave me three biscuits on a plate, settled the machine across his knees, and applauded me for perhaps ten seconds. I stood by the table with my coat on. I had spent years imagining the relief of passing, and now I found I was embarrassed enough to laugh.

He laughed too, which spoiled his rhythm.

Afterward, I asked about the recital.

“Saturday.”

“Ready?”

“Mechanically.”

The following week, I knocked to ask how it had gone.

He said his grandson had played beautifully, then admitted that the boy had stopped halfway through and asked to begin again.

“Did they let him?”

“Of course.”

“And the hand?”

“Dropped it getting out of the taxi.”

He showed me a crack along the wooden base. His daughter was coming to repair it on Sunday.

“Did you manage?”

“Oh, there were plenty of people.”

He said it lightly, but I thought of him sitting among all those busy hands with his own resting on a broken machine.

I nearly offered to go with him next time. Then I worried that this would be an enormous offer, involving years of school concerts and lectures about bats, and said nothing.

At my door, I reconsidered.

I went back downstairs and asked whether there was anything on before Sunday.

He consulted the noticeboard.

“Thursday. Local history. The old railway station.”

“I could do Thursday.”

“It may be quite dull.”

“That’s all right.”

He took a pencil from beside the telephone and wrote my name on the ticket.

We attended eleven things together that winter. The railway lecture was excellent. The poetry was not. At a production of *King Lear*, he leaned over during the interval and whispered, with unmistakable professional interest, “Those are her swords.”

His daughter fixed the machine. He brought it along, folded in a canvas bag, but usually left it there.

We got quite good.
